name: Dr. Football US
_comment_group: One of the shows under the Snapchat heading. The heading names the
network these frames are cut FOR and the channel is the show they are
cut from, so another show cutting for the same network is one more
folder under it rather than a heading of its own.
Like every channel under this heading it is a frame fetcher rather
than a thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of
vertical stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said
It is cut to Hall of Femme's design, which is the pack to read first:
the frame fetch, the vertical output, the transcription, the rewrite,
the card at the foot of the frame and every number in that card are
that pack's, and this one repeats none of them. What makes it this
show instead of that one is the face, the colour of the card and the
two colours the user may swap between.
It is also the first of four packs set in League Spartan - Oh My Goal,
Oh My Goal News and Soccer Stories FR are the others, and each is this
pack with its own two colours. How a word is picked out on them is
argued here once and pointed at from all three, because it is an
argument about the FACE and the face is what the four of them share.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.
_comment_title: What separates this show from the others under the heading is one
sentence long: it is set in League Spartan, on a deep indigo card, in
two colours the user picks per frame.
Everything else - the size, where the lines break, the capitals, the
shape of the card, where it stands on the frame - is the Snapchat
caption design and is stated once, in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json. This pack states only what
League Spartan is a geometric sans built on the circle, with a wide
round O and a tall x-height, and set in capitals at 40px it is the
blunt, even, poster-like line that sports captions have always been
set in. The app carries one cut of it and one only (see the face
pack), which is no shortcoming at caption size on a card - a geometric
face is at its most legible exactly where it is least decorated - but
it is what decides the highlight below.

_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set in
until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of its
own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to (see
state.textColorFor). It is one of the two in `colors` below, so
the white swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an untouched
frame - the swatch is found by matching this value rather than by
Absolute white rather than an off-white, and here the exact value
matters: the card behind it is a saturated mid-dark indigo, and
anything short of #FFFFFF on it reads as a caption that has faded
rather than as white type. There is nothing for a true white to be
too harsh against - it is sitting on a colour somebody chose, not
White letters on the indigo card is the pairing this show opens
on: the indigo is the brand, so it is the CARD - the shape that is
a fifth of the frame and reads before anything on it - and the
type is what has to stay legible against it.
_comment_colors: The two colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the card behind them - two buttons in each of the two rows in
the title panel (see editor.renderColorButtons).
Two colours rather than Hall of Femme's four, and that is the
brand rather than a shortened version of it. This show has one
colour and a white, so the palette is the pairing and its inverse:
indigo card with white type, or white card with indigo type.
Nothing counts the lists - the panel draws a swatch per entry and
the row wraps - so a row of two is a row of two.
The same two in both lists, deliberately, which is what every pack
under this heading does and for their reason: the point is the
PAIRING, and two rows written the same way read as one palette
offered twice rather than as two unrelated sets.
Nothing stops the user setting white on white. That is not an
oversight either: the lists are independent because the pairing is
the feature, and a rule barring the two matching combinations
would cost the panel more explaining than an invisible caption
costs the user, who can see it is invisible and presses another
swatch.
Two lists written, and three rows in the panel. A pack that names
no `highlight` list offers the picked words the letters' list (see
buildChannel in js/channels.js), so the third question - what
colour are the picked words - is asked here too, from these same
two colours.
_comment_highlight: The preset's word highlight, set in the block's own face and its
own white. Picked words are told apart by COLOUR, and the colour
is the user's, from the highlight row every palette now carries.
Until that row is pressed on a frame, a picked word looks exactly
like its neighbours and follows the letters' colour.
This pack used to switch the highlight off outright, and the
argument below is why - kept, because the half of it about the
face is still true and still decides that the picked words are
told apart by colour and not by cut. The half that is not true
any more is the second bullet: a picked word in the palette's
other colour IS the card's colour, but which colour the card is,
and whether there is a card at all, are now both the user's to
choose per frame (see the crossed-out swatch on the background
row). A split nobody can see is a pairing the user can see is
wrong and presses another swatch, as with white on white. Written
down once, for all nine packs that made this change, in
content/README.md under 'Every palette offers the picked words
too'.
Every sibling under this heading picks a word out by changing its
CUT and keeping its colour. Hall of Femme sets its captions in
Telegraf UltraLight and a picked word in UltraBold, Determined and
Fight Source swap an Open Sans for its bold, Fitness Story runs
Hanken Grotesk's two ends against each other. That is why the
preset chooses colour mode over box mode in the first place - the
words are already on a solid ground of their own, so a rectangle
behind them would be a shape inside a shape, and the change of cut
is loud enough without one.
This channel has no second cut to change to. The app carries one
weight of League Spartan, the show is set in League Spartan, and
that is the whole of the family available to it. Neither way round
that is worth having:
- A synthesised bold is a stroke laid over letters drawn without
one, and it is MEASURED as well as drawn - the caption would be
laid out against a face nobody chose, which is the failure
fontguard exists to catch, only self-inflicted.
- A picked word in the palette's other colour is the CARD's
colour, and on the card that is a picked word nobody can see.
- A box behind the picked word would work, but it is a second
shape inside the card and a second thing for the user to
colour.
The day a second weight of League Spartan is dropped into fonts/
this channel can have Hall of Femme's highlight exactly - a second
face pack, `highlight.face` naming it, and nothing else changes.
The `color` is stated rather than inherited only because it says
so out loud: the skeleton's is the same white.
_comment_panel: Deep indigo, and the fill is the one thing about the card this
pack decides: its shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow
are the Snapchat caption design and come from the preset.
It is the first entry in `colors.panel` above as well, so the
swatch that shows as chosen on an untouched frame is the one at
the start of the row. Nothing requires that - the swatch is found
by matching this value rather than by being listed first - and the
type's own colour is deliberately NOT first in its row, which is
the same freedom used the other way round.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient. It exists to hold a title legible against the
photograph, and this title is not against the photograph at all - it
is on a card of its own. A scrim over every still would darken forty
pictures to solve a problem the card has already solved.
